extracted.intended_audience: Organizations and collaborative teams applying for the NEH Scholarly Editions and Translations grant (universities, libraries, historical societies, research institutes, etc.)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for preparing and submitting applications for NEH's Scholarly Editions and Translations program supporting collaborative editorial and translation projects in the humanities. Covers eligible subject areas, required scholarly content, funding levels, period of performance, allowable costs, and application procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligible subject focus
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2026-27 Scholarly Editions and Translations competition will accept only editions and translations projects in American history and culture or Western civilization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications must focus on topics in the history and culture of the United States in any period from the Colonial Era to the present, or topics in Western civilization from antiquity to the present. Use examples of previously funded projects (e.g., Papers of George Washington, Collected Papers of Albert Einstein) to judge fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project purpose and uniqueness (foundational texts / adequacy of existing editions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Supports collaborative teams who edit, annotate, and translate foundational humanities texts that are vital to generating new scholarship but are not available in adequate editions or translations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects should demonstrate that the target text(s) are foundational and that current editions/translations are inadequate. The program has historically funded major editorial and translation projects; applicants should position their work relative to existing scholarship and editions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required scholarly additions (introductions, annotations, critical apparatus)
rubrics_metrics.description: All editions and translations must contain additional and new scholarly material such as introductions, annotations, and critical apparatus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The grant does not fund simple reprints or bare translations; proposals must include substantial new scholarly content (e.g., critical apparatus, commentary, explanatory annotation) appropriate to the edition or translation chosen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable outputs (formats)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expected Output: Annotated Edition; Annotated Translation; Digital Edition; Print Volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editions and translations may be print, digital, or a combination of both. Select the format(s) that best deliver the required scholarly apparatus and justify format choices in the application narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding levels and award amounts
rubrics_metrics.description: The program includes three funding levels: Planning, Implementation, and Chairman’s Special Awards in American History and Culture. Maximum award amount: $300,000 in outright funds; up to $450,000 may be available if requesting at least $150,000 in matching funds. Up to $1 million for Chairman’s Special Awards in American History and Culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the appropriate funding level and budget carefully. Increasing award amount may require matching funds; Chairman's Special Awards have higher caps and different expectations. Consult the Notice of Funding Opportunity for level-specific requirements and restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Period of performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Period of performance: One to three years. For a Chairman’s Special Award, you must request a period of performance of five years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects must plan activities that fit within the stated period. The program supports continuous full-time or part-time activities over the awarded period; timeline and staffing should reflect continuous work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant type / organizational eligibility
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants are organizations (e.g., universities, libraries, archives, scholarly societies). Register for a SAM number and an account on Grants.gov; both are required. Ensure institutional eligibility and current registrations before applying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project team and collaboration expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Supports collaborative teams who edit, annotate, and translate foundational humanities texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assemble a team with demonstrated editorial and translation expertise and appropriate consultants. The program notes opportunities for international collaboration (e.g., U.S.-based scholars working with scholars in Israel may have additional funding opportunities via Partnership Opportunity Notifications). Describe roles, qualifications, and collaborative arrangements clearly in the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowable project expenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical project expenses include salary for editorial and research activities, travel to collections to verify source material, and consultant fees for translation, editorial work, and the implementation of a digital edition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build a budget that aligns with these typical allowable costs; justify travel and consultant needs tied directly to the edition/translation work. Consult the Notice of Funding Opportunity for budget rules and restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital edition implementation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Editions and translations may be digital, and projects may include implementation of a digital edition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If proposing a digital edition, address technical implementation, sustainability, and how the digital format will present the required scholarly apparatus. Consultant fees for digital implementation are allowable; provide plans for hosting, preservation, and user access as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application materials and procedural requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must follow the instructions outlined in the Notice of Funding Opportunity and Grants.gov application package; resources include the Notice of Funding Opportunity (PDF), Grants.gov application package, Frequently Asked Questions (PDF), sample application narratives, and program resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the NOFO exactly when assembling the application. Register with SAM.gov and Grants.gov; download Adobe Reader; follow tips for creating PDFs. Submit via Grants.gov and verify receipt by checking the multiple confirmation emails Grants.gov sends (they may appear in spam). Use sample narratives and awarded project examples for structuring the proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with NEH policies (including AI policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications are subject to NEH policies, including the Policy on the Use of Artificial Intelligence for NEH Grant Proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review and comply with all NEH policies referenced in the program resources. Explicitly address any policy-relevant elements (e.g., use of AI in preparing materials) as required in the NOFO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of continuous project activity
rubrics_metrics.description: The program supports continuous full-time or part-time activities during a period of performance of one to three years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Project narratives, staffing plans, and timelines should demonstrate continuous work (either full- or part-time) rather than intermittent or one-off activities. Show how deliverables will be produced within the awarded period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples of previously funded projects as models
rubrics_metrics.description: The program provides examples of projects funded by this grant program (e.g., The Papers of George Washington; The Works of Giuseppe Verdi; The Collected Papers of Albert Einstein).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult sample application narratives and awarded projects to understand the scale, scope, scholarly apparatus, and formats that NEH has funded. Use these as models for setting ambition and structuring the proposal.
